A US court found Google’s search business to be a monopoly because it violated Section 2 of the Sherman Act by engaging in exclusionary conduct through default-distribution deals [Source: ev-1]. Specifically, Judge Amit Mehta ruled on August 5, 2024, that Google was a monopolist in general search services and general search text advertising due to its practice of paying companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla billions of dollars to remain their default search engine [Source: ev-1]. This created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generated scale, which produced data that improved quality, thereby protecting the default status against rivals [Source: ev-1]. Evidence showed that Google paid approximately $26.3 billion for distribution in 2021, including roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue to Apple [Source: ev-1].

On August 5, 20 marking the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000, Judge Mehta ordered structural remedies requiring Google to sell its Chrome browser and cease paying for default search placement through no longer allowing revenue-sharing agreements [Source: ev-1]. Additionally, the ruling imposed limits on Google’s acquisitions and AI-related investments [Source: ev-1]. Google appealed this decision to the DC Circuit in 2025, arguing that the trial court punished procompetitive innovation, with the final outcome remaining pending as of 2025 [Source: ev-1].
